Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti (also published as Alhassan Datti Mohammed and Alhassan Mohammed Datti) is the most senior consultant in the Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital, and one of the pioneering anaesthetists of Kano and Jigawa States.

title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
Training
Prof. Datti trained in anaesthesia from 1997 to 2003 at the University of Ibadan and University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan — Nigeria’s oldest teaching hospital — where he obtained the Postgraduate Diploma in Anaesthesia. He went on to become a Fellow of the West African College of Surgeons (WACS) in Anaesthesia in 2007, the first Fellow of the College from either Kano or Jigawa State in Northwest Nigeria.

title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
Work and interests
Prof. Datti’s career has combined clinical anaesthesia with public-health research and regional capacity-building:

He served as principal investigator on a study, conducted with PRRINN‑MNCH (Partnership for Reviving Routine Immunisation in Northern Nigeria — Maternal, Newborn and Child Health), examining the impact of access to safe, reliable general anaesthesia on emergency obstetric care and neonatal outcomes.
He documented AKTH’s transition from ketamine-only to inhalational general anaesthesia, and has spoken on this experience at international meetings, including the All‑Africa Anaesthesia Congress.
He coordinated a partnership between the Liberian Dental Association, the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists, and AKTH to train Liberian physicians toward the WACS Diploma in Anaesthesia (DA), addressing a critical shortage of physician anaesthesia providers in Liberia.
He has co-authored multiple peer-reviewed studies from the department, spanning obstetric anaesthesia, patient knowledge and perception of anaesthesia, and drug-dosing research relevant to routine practice in a resource-constrained setting.

title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
Leadership Beyond the Department
Prof. Datti is the incumbent President of the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists (NSA) and has worked tirelessly to bring transformative changes to the association.
He also served as President-Elect of the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists (2022–2024 Executive Committee).

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text: Departmental seminar series · Presented by Amina Nura Yakasai · Moderator: Dr Bello · Open to all departmental staff

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Overview
Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) is a systematic, multimodal approach to perioperative care aimed at reducing the immense surgical stress on the patient and facilitating early recovery. Pioneered by Prof. Kehlet and Wilmore, the ERAS Study Group was established and later formalized as the ERAS Society in 2010. The first consensus guidelines appeared for colorectal surgeries in 2005, radical cystectomy in 2013, and gynecological and bariatric surgery in 2016.
ERAS represents a shift from reactive to proactive patient management — a careful, coordinated multidisciplinary approach that, when adhered to, delivers better clinical outcomes.

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Aims of ERAS
Enhanced recovery is a combination of elements of care for elective surgery which aims to:

Optimise pre-operative preparation for surgery
Avoid iatrogenic problems such as postoperative ileus
Minimise the stress response to surgery
Speed recovery and return to normal function
Early recognition of abnormal recovery and intervention if necessary

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
The Enhanced Recovery Pathway
The pathway starts with the decision to seek surgical opinion and continues through follow-up of the patient after discharge. It aims at identifying and managing risk factors and comorbidities, and encompasses five phases: pre-operative, intra-operative, immediate post-operative, late post-operative, and recovery at home.

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Prehabilitation: Preparing for Surgery
Preoperative preparation is the foundation of ERAS:

Patient counselling and involvement in decision making — through verbal discussion, written pamphlets, and online websites. Check understanding of expectations of post-operative recovery (joint responsibility).
Correction of nutritional deficiencies (anaemia) — in malnourished patients, start treatment 7–10 days before surgery and continue enteral solutions for at least 8 weeks postoperatively.
Exercise training, relaxation strategies, and sleep hygiene.


Fasting Guidelines (NPO Time)

Solid food: up to 6 hours before induction of anaesthesia
Clear liquid: up to 2 hours before induction — helps to prevent the catabolic state



Carbohydrate Loading
Oral complex carbohydrates (maltodextrin) with high concentration (12.5%):

100 gm (800 ml) administered the night before surgery
50 gm (400 ml) 2–3 hours before induction of anaesthesia

Benefits: lessen discomfort and anxiety, maintain lean body mass and muscle strength, accelerate return of bowel function, and reduce insulin resistance.


Thromboprophylaxis
Thromboembolism carries significant morbidity and mortality. Prophylaxis includes:

Mechanical devices: compressive stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression devices
Anticoagulants: LMWH, unfragmented heparin



Preoperative Medication

Premedication as per requirement — aim is to reduce surgical stress response, without any sedative properties (or short-acting)
Pain management: acetaminophen, NSAIDs, gabapentinoids, dexamethasone
Shorter-acting pre-medications (alpha-2 agonists, beta blockers) — improve pain relief, anticatabolic, reduce blood loss and PONV
Avoid hyperglycaemia (hypermetabolic stress response increases risk of infection and cardiovascular morbidity) and hypoglycaemia



Antibiotic Prophylaxis

A single dose covering both aerobes and anaerobes, administered just before surgical incision (30–60 minutes before)
A second dose for procedures lasting > 4 hours or blood loss > 1500 ml
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin wipes pre-incision, bowel preparation with antibiotics, glove/instrument change, and antibiotic irrigation prior to closure — reduces SSIs by 34%
Improves immune function and reduces inflammatory markers

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Intra-operative Management

Anaesthetic Techniques

Pre-emptive analgesia — modify nociception and maximise physiological and pharmacological benefits to promote quick recovery
Oxygen titration — maintain PaO2 level (avoid hyperoxia)
Lung-protective mechanical ventilation
Reduced volatile anaesthetics (0.7–1.3 MAC) — monitoring depth with BIS 40–60 and end-tidal concentration
Avoid nitrous oxide (PONV, accumulates in third cavities, increases thrombotic morbidity)
Short- and medium-acting neuromuscular agents
Anaesthetic drugs with minimal post-operative hangover effect on gastric motility



Intravascular Status and Fluid Management
Optimise fluid management — maintain central euvolaemia (avoid interstitial shift), minimise salt and water excess (vasopressors to be used). Balanced crystalloids are recommended.

Zero-balance fluid therapy (low-risk patient, low-risk surgery): 1–3 ml/kg/hr of balanced salt solution (maintain preop body weight, > 2.5 kg)
Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) (high-risk patient, large intravascular volume loss): using minimally invasive cardiac output monitor or oesophageal doppler; judicious use of colloids; inotropes if cardiac index < 2.5 l/min



Avoiding Hypothermia
Hypothermia causes delayed wound healing, increased infection, increased blood loss, increased cortisol levels, increased oxygen consumption, and extends action of anaesthetic drugs.

Active warming devices in all cases lasting > 30 minutes (core temp maintained within 0.5–1.5 C of normal under GA)
Forced air warming systems, warmed IV and irrigated solutions
Anti-shivering agents: pethidine 0.25–0.5 mg/kg, tramadol, clonidine, dexmedetomidine, magnesium sulphate



Minimising Surgical Drains and Catheters

Nasogastric tubes — prolong paralytic ileus, predispose to pulmonary aspiration
Urinary catheters — remove as early as possible irrespective of epidural catheter

Lower abdominal/pelvic surgeries: within 72 hours
Most other surgeries: within 24 hours
(CAUTI risk increases by 5% per day)

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Post-operative Care

Early and Adequate Nutrition
Decreased ileus, enhanced wound healing, reduced infection, maintained muscle strength.

Early enteral nutrition — return to normal fluids and diets as soon as tolerated
Discontinue IV fluids when drinking (> 1.5 l/day)
High-protein diet (> 50% of protein/kcal)
Benefits of immunonutrition: arginine, glutamine, omega-3 fatty acids, and nucleotides



Early Mobility
Patient empowerment through written targets, preoperative physical activity, and record keeping. Reduces skeletal muscle loss, improves respiratory function, and decreases pulmonary and thromboembolic complications.

Sit out of bed for 2 hours on the day of surgery and 6 hours a day until discharge
Daily procedure-specific goals
Physiotherapy and rehabilitation is vital
Discharge when criteria are met

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Limitations

Fear of complications (e.g. aspiration risk)
Logistic issues
Illiteracy
Inability to recognise early warning signs
Lack of trained personnel
Poor telecommunications
Lack of coordination among multispecialty teams
Infrastructure-related issues

title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)
text:
Conclusion
The application of ERAS has certainly changed perioperative practice to provide a smoother journey for patients throughout the perioperative period of stress. ERAS is simply a careful, coordinated multidisciplinary approach, adherence to which has better clinical outcomes.
In patients undergoing craniotomy, considerations such as techniques for scalp blocks, non-opioid alternatives for pain control, and improved outcomes with minimally invasive surgery are little different from the traditional ERAS concept.

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
1 Why a structured handover matters
Verbal handovers that aren’t structured tend to omit items unpredictably — often exactly the detail that matters for the next few hours of care. A short, consistent structure reduces that risk without adding much time to a busy transfer. This mirrors the logic behind the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, which was shown to reduce post-operative morbidity and mortality across a range of hospital settings when used consistently (Haynes et al. 2009; Safe Surgery Saves Lives Study Group 2009).

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
2 Suggested handover structure

Patient identification & background — name, age, parity, key obstetric history, indication for surgery.
Procedure performed — type of anaesthesia, surgical procedure, any intra-operative complications.
Haemodynamic course — blood loss, fluids and blood products given, vasopressor use, any instability and how it was managed.
Airway and respiratory status — extubation status, oxygen requirement, any airway concerns for the ICU team to be aware of.
Analgesia plan — what has been given, what is prescribed next, and any regional technique in place (e.g. spinal opioid, wound catheter).
Outstanding concerns and thresholds for escalation — specifically what should prompt the ICU team to call anaesthesia back.

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
3 Using this guide
This is a teaching resource for residents, not a substitute for local protocol. Departments should adapt the sequence to match their own documentation and handover tools, and residents should confirm current local practice with their supervising consultant.

title: Marking World Anaesthesia Day at AKTH
text:
Every year on 16 October, the anaesthesia community marks World Anaesthesia Day, commemorating the first successful public demonstration of ether anaesthesia in 1846.
At AKTH, the department used the day to run a short in-house symposium for residents, nurse anaesthetists and theatre staff, focused on:

title: Marking World Anaesthesia Day at AKTH
text:
A shared global effort
Observances like this connect our department to the wider work of the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists and the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists, both of which promote safe anaesthesia access worldwide — a reminder that safe surgery and anaesthesia remain out of reach for many patients globally, and that local diligence contributes to a much larger effort.
Thank you to every member of the peri-operative team who took part.

A checklist is only useful if it prompts a genuine review rather than a box-ticking exercise. On our unit, the checklist is read aloud during the consultant-led round, with the bedside nurse and resident confirming each item against the patient in front of them — not from memory.

text:

KEYWORDS · REGIONAL ANAESTHESIA · ULTRASOUND · NERVE BLOCKS · TRAINING

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
1 Probe selection

Linear (high-frequency) probes — best for superficial structures (nerves within ~4 cm), such as interscalene, supraclavicular, and forearm blocks. Better resolution, less penetration.
Curvilinear (low-frequency) probes — needed for deeper structures, such as the sciatic nerve at the gluteal level or in larger patients.

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
2 Needle visualisation

In-plane technique keeps the entire needle shaft visible along the probe’s long axis — generally the easier technique to learn first, as the needle tip position is continuously seen.
Out-of-plane technique shows the needle only as a bright dot crossing the beam — faster for some experienced operators, but easier to lose track of the tip as a beginner.
Small, deliberate needle movements — rather than large sweeps — make it far easier to keep the tip in view.

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
3 Common early pitfalls

Chasing the needle with the probe instead of keeping the probe still and adjusting the needle trajectory — this usually makes tip tracking worse, not better.
Mistaking the needle shadow for the tip — the brightest point on screen is not always the true tip; small in-and-out jiggles or a burst of local anaesthetic (hydrolocation) can help confirm true tip position.
Poor gel contact at the probe edges, distorting the image exactly where the needle is entering.

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Overview
This seminar provides a foundational introduction to artificial intelligence (AI), explainable AI (xAI), ethical AI, and collaborative intelligence, with a focus on their application in healthcare. Delivered as Module 1 of the Resident Doctors Weekly Seminar series at the Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital, the lecture covers data fundamentals, the AI landscape, ethical and legal frameworks, and the emerging paradigm of human-AI collaboration.

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
section: Part 1: Data — The Foundation of AI
text:
Part 1: Data — The Foundation of AI

What Is Data?
Data is derived from the Latin word datum, meaning fact. It exists in two main formats — structured and unstructured — and can be quantitative or qualitative. As The Economist noted in 2017, “The world’s most valuable resource is no longer oil, but data.”


Oil vs. Data

Infinite vs. finite: Oil is scarce and depletable; data can be duplicated and used infinitely without disappearing.
Depreciation: Oil retains energy value over time, but data often depreciates rapidly as information becomes outdated.
Silos vs. spills: Oil spills cause immediate environmental damage; data “spills” come as massive privacy breaches and security hacks.



Value of Data in Healthcare
Approximately 1 billion people use wearable technologies like smartwatches, fitness bands, and medical devices. Physicians can use the data generated to detect and predict possible disorders, improving decision-making in medicine and patient care. These data also drive pharmaceutical and healthcare research globally.


The 5 V’s of Big Data

Volume — the sheer quantity of data
Velocity — the speed at which data is generated and processed
Variety — the diversity of data types and sources
Veracity — the accuracy and trustworthiness of data
Value — the useful insights that can be extracted



Data Growth

2010: approximately 2 Zettabytes (1 ZB = 1 billion terabytes)
2021: 80 Zettabytes
2025: 182 Zettabytes
Forecasted to reach 394 Zettabytes by 2028



Types of Data Used in AI

Structured data: Quantitative, organized in rows and columns (spreadsheets). Examples: names, dates, addresses, credit card numbers, stock information.
Unstructured data (dark data): Qualitative data such as medical records, images, text, audio. Makes up over 80% of all modern data generated globally.
Semi-structured data: Combines features of both; uses metadata to identify characteristics and scale data into records. Examples: JSON files, XML code, emails with distinct headers but open text bodies.



DIKW — From Raw Data to Valuable Decisions
The DIKW model is a four-layer framework:

Data: Raw facts (e.g. 90, 1.6, Risk, Hypertension)
Information: Contextualized data (e.g. 70 kg, 1.6 m, risk of hypertension)
Knowledge: Interpreted information (e.g. BMI is 35.2 kg/m², increased health risk)
Wisdom: Actionable insight (e.g. weight reduction is needed due to attendant health risks)



Data Storage Stages and Data Pipelines
Data travels through a structured pipeline from creation to consumption. The three core storage architectures are Data Lakes, Data Warehouses, and Data Lakehouses — the modern hybrid.

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Part 2: Introduction to AI

What Is AI?
Artificial intelligence refers to the simulation of human intelligence processes by computer systems. These processes include learning, reasoning, and self-correction.


Types of AI

Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI): Task-specific AI (e.g. voice assistants, recommendation engines)
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): Hypothetical AI with human-level cognitive abilities across all domains
Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI): Hypothetical AI surpassing human intelligence



Machine Learning
Machine learning is a subset of AI where systems learn from data without being explicitly programmed. Key approaches include:

Supervised learning: Learning from labelled data
Unsupervised learning: Finding patterns in unlabelled data
Reinforcement learning: Learning through trial and error with rewards



Deep Learning
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning using artificial neural networks with multiple layers. It powers image recognition, natural language processing, and many modern AI applications.


AI in Healthcare
AI applications in healthcare include:

Medical imaging and diagnostics
Drug discovery and development
Personalized treatment plans
Clinical decision support
Predictive analytics for patient outcomes
Robotic surgery assistance

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Part 3: Explainable AI (xAI)

What Is xAI?
Explainable AI (xAI) is a set of processes, methods, and tools that allows human users to comprehend, trust, and effectively manage the outputs of machine learning algorithms. Traditional deep learning models operate as a “black box” — they ingest massive amounts of data, run it through billions of hidden mathematical layers, and output predictions, but cannot explain why they made a specific decision. xAI aims to turn that black box into a “glass box” by making internal reasoning visible and understandable.


Why xAI Is Necessary
When AI was only used for recommending movies on Netflix, a lack of explanation did not matter. Today, AI systems make high-stakes decisions that directly impact human lives, making explanations legally, ethically, and operationally mandatory.
Example in medical diagnostics: If an AI scans an X-ray and flags a tumor, doctors cannot blindly trust the tool. They need to know exactly which pixels or patterns led the AI to that conclusion before operating.


The Trade-Off: Accuracy vs. Explainability

Simple models (linear regression, basic decision trees): 100% explainable, but too weak for complex tasks
Advanced models (transformers, deep neural networks): massive accuracy, but billions of parameters make them incredibly difficult for humans to map out



Historical Failures Caused by Lack of xAI

The UK’s A-Level grading algorithm for national high school exams during COVID-19
Epic Systems’ Sepsis Prediction Model failure



Mechanistic Interpretability
Researchers are mapping out specific features across millions of neurons simultaneously. Pioneered by teams at Anthropic and OpenAI, this field attempts to reverse-engineer neural networks the same way a neuroscientist studies a physical brain.

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Part 4: Ethical AI

Core Ethical Principles
The following principles guide the development, deployment, and use of AI:

Fairness: AI systems should treat all individuals equally and avoid any form of discrimination
Accountability: Someone should always be accountable for the outcomes of an AI system
Transparency: Decisions made by AI systems should be explainable and comprehensible



The HamurabiAi Case Study
A fictional healthcare AI company illustrates how ethical principles apply in practice:

Fairness challenge: AI system develops social biases, discriminating based on gender, ethnicity, occupation. Solution: Continuously test AI systems to detect and rectify bias.
Accountability challenge: When the system makes a mistake, who is responsible — the developer, doctor, patient, hospital, or company? Solution: Define clear responsibilities for each AI system’s outcomes.
Transparency challenge: The system recommends a treatment without explaining why. Was it a black box or explainable AI model? Solution: Make AI systems explainable; share knowledge among stakeholders.



AI Ethics and Legislation — The Way Forward

Adopt a proactive approach involving all stakeholders: patients, healthcare providers, financial sponsors, researchers, regulators
Develop clear guidelines and intellectual discussions on harnessing AI’s potential in healthcare
Regulatory bodies must work harmoniously towards detailed ethical and legal guidelines
Regularly review understanding of ethical and legal concerns as AI systems evolve



Nigerian AI Policies and Legislation

National AI Strategy: The Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy launched the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS)
Pending Legislation: Control of Usage of AI Technology Bill and National AI and Robotic Sciences Bill
Regulatory Baselines: NITDA Draft Code of Practice for AI, introducing rules on algorithmic transparency, safety risk assessments, and human oversight
National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR): Established in 2020
Data Protection: Nigeria Data Protection Regulation 2019 (NDPR), Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA)



AI Ethical Guidelines
Most guidelines contain variations of:

Humans need control and oversight of AI
AI systems need to be technically robust and safe
Respect principles of privacy, data governance, transparency, and fairness
Environment and societal well-being
Clear accountability framework

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Part 5: Collaborative Intelligence

What Is Collaborative Intelligence (CI)?
Neither a human brain nor an AI algorithm can achieve perfect accuracy and precision. CI — also known as hybrid intelligence — is the practice of combining human and artificial intelligence to solve problems, innovate, and make decisions. It applies AI solutions to augment human productivity, helping individuals, teams, organisations, and businesses realise their full potential.
The key shift: think in terms of “Humans and AI” and not “Humans or AI.”


The Evolution of CI

Recent fears about AI replacing humans at work gave the impression AI was a threat to jobs
Developments show the focus should be on leveraging advantages offered by both AI and humans
This overcomes the weaknesses of either alone while strengthening both together



Impact of CI in the Workplace

Enhanced decision-making
Accelerated innovation
Improved problem-solving
Increased productivity
Enhanced learning and skill development



CI in Healthcare
The increasing burden and complexity of disease cannot be managed in a one-to-one relationship by the decreasing clinical workforce. CI:

Mirrors the potential and limits of leveraging AI in clinical care
Involves advanced analytics and computing power
Humans bear responsibility for accuracy, completeness, and inherent bias in training data
Has already transformed radiology
Will allow ingestion of information beyond imaging to be integrated across specialties



Why CI Is Important in Healthcare
The current healthcare challenge has three components:

Accelerating complexity and exponential information overload
Transition to continuous care models and optimized resource allocation
Eradicating disparities in access and quality, including social determinants of health



Physician Responsibility and Interactivity With Technology

Clinicians must become active in understanding the role of AI in healthcare
Must deploy critical thinking skills to evaluate AI-sourced information
Must be involved in the digital transformation of healthcare using AI
As AI in clinical decision-making evolves, explainable AI principles must be adopted



Clinical Applications of CI

Clinicians need to understand what part of the process the AI aims to address
Start small — use CI for low-complexity, non-urgent care first
Clinicians must be involved in algorithm development
At population level, CI aids in identifying individuals with rising risk
Final implementation of care always lies with the clinical team, with shared decision-making with the patient



Successful Collaborations

IBM Watson for Oncology: Invaluable tool for oncologists
Google Health and Royal Surrey County Hospital (UK): Improved breast cancer detection using AI in mammogram readings
Babylon Health: Telemedicine services enhancing patient care through human-AI collaboration
Stanford University School of Medicine: ML models analysing patient vital signs and EHR data to identify patients at risk of sepsis, respiratory failure, and cardiac arrest



Challenges in Human-AI Collaboration

Lack of trust between practitioners and AI “black boxes”
Outdated infrastructure and lack of interoperability
Resistance by healthcare workers to learn new technologies
Fear of job loss
Ethical challenges including patient privacy, data security, and algorithmic bias

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
section: Part 6: High-Risk Use Cases and AI Fluency
text:
Part 6: High-Risk Use Cases and AI Fluency

High-Risk Use Cases
Some use cases pose elevated risk because they influence domains vital to public welfare. For these, additional safety measures apply:

Human-in-the-loop: A qualified professional must review content or decisions before dissemination
Disclosure: If model outputs are presented to individuals, AI involvement must be disclosed

Examples of high-risk use cases: Legal, healthcare, insurance, finance, employment and housing, academic writing/testing/accreditation, research, media or professional journalistic content.


AI Use in Academics — Current Journal Policies (2025–2026)
Publishers classify AI use into three frameworks:

Assistive (grammar checking, language polishing, reference formatting): No disclosure required — treated like spell-checkers
Generative (generating text, figures, code, literature synthesis): Disclosure mandatory upon submission
Prohibitive (AI as author, undisclosed generative use, AI content as original analysis): Not allowed



AI Fluency and the 4D Framework
AI fluency is the ability to collaborate effectively with AI tools — developing judgement to use AI well across different situations. The 4D Framework identifies four core competencies for effective AI interaction.

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Part 7: Prompt Engineering

What Is Prompt Engineering?
Prompt engineering is the art and science of designing, refining, and optimizing text instructions (prompts) to guide AI models like ChatGPT, DeepSeek, or Gemini to generate accurate, useful, and relevant responses. Think of it as “programming in natural language.”


General Rules
Speak to an AI chat app naturally, concisely, and conversationally, by:

Setting the stage (your role, objectives, and context)
Defining the task (what action you want the AI to take)
Specifying rules (tone, style, and examples)



Why It Matters
Large language models lack built-in task lists; their output depends almost entirely on how you ask.

Vague prompt: “Tell me about climate change.”
Engineered prompt: “Explain three major causes of climate change and their mechanisms. Include citations from peer-reviewed research and write for a 10th-grade reading level.”



Core Techniques

Provide context: Give the AI background information or a specific persona
Specify format: Tell the AI how to structure its answer (bullet points, table, essay)
Few-shot prompting: Provide examples of input and desired output
Chain-of-thought (CoT): Ask the AI to “think step-by-step” before giving its final answer
Define constraints: Tell the AI what not to do (e.g. “Do not hallucinate; stick to verifiable facts”)
Persona/role prompting: Assign a persona before asking (e.g. “You are a [expert role] with [X years experience]”)

title: Introduction to AI, xAI, Ethical AI and Collaborative Intelligence
text:
Conclusion and Recommendations

With great power comes great responsibility — ethics must guide AI adoption in healthcare
A good understanding of ethical and legal implications will help drive responsible AI use
There is an urgent need for clinicians to be actively involved in the design, development, deployment, and use of AI systems
AI must be developed in regulated partnership between clinicians and computer scientists
More doctors versed in both data science and medicine will be needed
A robust legal framework for AI in healthcare is essential, but regulation should not stifle innovation
As AI continues to evolve, we must embrace change and seize opportunities
